extracted.intended_audience: open-source investigators and researchers (Bellingcat/GLAN/J&A Unit) documenting potential IHL/ICL violations in Ukraine
extracted.subtask_description: Methodology and standards for conducting, recording, preserving and presenting open-source investigations into alleged violations of international humanitarian law and international criminal law in Ukraine for potential legal use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pursue all lines of reasonable enquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: The requirement to pursue all lines of reasonable enquiry including those leading towards evidence that may explain the attack or suggest alternative attribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigators must try to establish, with an open mind, what happened and actively search for information which could explain an attack or suggest alternative attribution (often described as ‘exculpatory evidence’). Ensure to investigate all possible explanations; use your Table of Factual Inquiries to identify relevant lines of inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search for exculpatory evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigators must actively search for information which could explain an attack or suggest alternative attribution (evidence that excuses or explains the incident).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exculpatory evidence could include evidence of military targets present before/during attack (fighters, checkpoints, military bases, weapons stores), or information that casts doubt on presumptions about responsibility. Because investigations often occur before charges are brought, treat such material as potentially exculpatory and record searches accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record searches and online activity (search-term logs & Hunchly)
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain a log of search terms in addition to using Hunchly, which tracks your online activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This demonstrates how you found relevant content and shows whether you carried out an unbiased search and pursued all lines of inquiry. Keep explicit search-term logs alongside automated tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use VPNs and clear cookies / standardise research starting point
rubrics_metrics.description: Use VPNs and clear cookies before creating new research accounts to create a standardised starting point for what search algorithms return.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measures are taken out of an abundance of caution to reduce algorithmic personalization effects on search results; note the extent of algorithmic influence may be limited but these steps help reproducibility and demonstrate care.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retain all potentially relevant content for disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Retain background information and records that could be relevant for disclosure to a defendant or prosecution review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure threshold is material that “can reasonably be considered capable of undermining the prosecution case or assisting the defence.” Examples (from SO15) include anything that casts doubt on witness reliability, motives for false allegations, materials affecting admissibility, evidence pointing to other persons, rough drafts, notes, emails. Not all retained material will meet the threshold—only material that could undermine/assist must be disclosed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record investigator communications and decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep records of investigator communications and decisions, including any discussion about ignoring information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Records that show agreement to ignore information or comments revealing bias could be disclosable. Preserve chats, decision notes, and editorial discussions; consider external counsel or in-house disclosure review before handing materials to prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Hunchly and Google Docs to create an auditable record
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Hunchly to track online activity and Google Docs change history to retain information about changes in drafts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hunchly creates a record of browsing and captures pages; Google Docs retains draft histories which may be scrutinised in disclosure reviews. Be mindful that these tools also capture irrelevant content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve digital evidence with an auditable chain of custody (use Mnemonic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Digital evidence should be preserved to enable a robust chain of custody to be demonstrated, using Mnemonic for immutable preservation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If unsure whether to enter an item into the preservation sheet, either enter it to be safe or consult the legal team. Preservation is essential for potential legal proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Uwazi for analysis but not as preservation
rubrics_metrics.description: Uwazi is an analysis database and does not perform preservation; e-log everything that could be relevant to an offence in Uwazi while preserving originals elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enter investigative work into Uwazi for analysis, but rely on preservation tools (Mnemonic) for immutable storage. Treat Uwazi entries as analytic records rather than evidentiary preservation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present findings in neutral, non-judgmental language
rubrics_metrics.description: Write information in neutral language, free from legal or moral commentary, to reinforce objectivity and provide a uniform basis for authorities or lawyers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the project's style guides and language recommendations to ensure uniformity. Do not offer expert opinion at the write-up stage; if you include opinions on authenticity or significance, use the recommended language guidance to qualify them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Produce comprehensive notes that enable retracing of analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Write-ups and research notes should be comprehensive enough that you or another person could retrace your steps, particularly if required to appear in court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid truncating analysis; include sufficient context, sources, timestamps and methodology to allow verification and re-walking of investigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand relevant legal frameworks (IHL and ICL)
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigators must have a basic understanding of international humanitarian law (IHL) and international criminal law (ICL) so they know what factual information is relevant to alleged violations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This enables development of lines of inquiry using common sense. Consult the Table of Factual Inquiries and the legal team for questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess target status under the principle of distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether attacked objects were military objectives or civilian objects by examining nature, location, purpose or use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A military objective is one that by nature, location, purpose or use makes an effective contribution to military action and whose neutralisation offers a definite military advantage. Investigate occupation of civilian locations (schools, hospitals) and thoroughly examine evidence that might indicate military use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise categories of IHL violations
rubrics_metrics.description: Be able to identify IHL violations such as deliberate targeting of civilians, indiscriminate strikes, disproportionate attacks, and failure to take feasible precautions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these categories to frame factual inquiries and tags in your database; understand how each category maps to potential Rome Statute offences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess obligations of precautions in attack
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the attacker satisfied obligations to: verify that objectives are not civilians, take feasible precautions in means/methods, refrain from attacks likely to violate proportionality, cancel or suspend attacks if risk appears, and offer advance warning when feasible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are distinct obligations; compliance is judged by what information was available to the decision-maker at the time of attack. Investigate what would have been visible/knowable to commanders or pilots (e.g., visible emblems, aerial view indicators).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess compliance based on attacker's information at time of decision
rubrics_metrics.description: Compliance with IHL is assessed based on the decision made by the commanding officer or pilot at the point when the attack was launched, not solely on consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate the information available to the attacker before/at the time of the attack (e.g., visible medical emblems, what a pilot could see from above) to assess whether precautions were taken.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine civilian status and direct participation in hostilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish whether persons present were civilians or members of armed forces and whether civilians took a direct part in hostilities (and thus were targetable for such time).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect evidence about activities of people on-scene (weapons, uniforms, badges, behaviour). Recognise the high threshold for 'direct participation' and use contextual indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify weapon types and methods of warfare
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify weapon types where possible since weapon type affects assessments of indiscriminate use, precision, expected destruction, links to parties, and whether intended target was hit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weapon identification helps evaluate proportionality, precautions, and possible attribution. Document whether weapons are precision-guided, area weapons, or prohibited types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document use of prohibited weapons and prohibited methods of warfare
rubrics_metrics.description: Be alert to absolutely prohibited weapon types and methods of warfare (reference Rule 71 ICRC Customary IHL Database and relevant treaties) and prohibited practices (starvation as a weapon, pillage, attacks on objects indispensable for civilians, refusing humanitarian access, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cluster munitions, while not customary-prohibited vis-à-vis Russia/Ukraine, are of high interest because of wide-area effects and long-term danger. Record weapon indicators, remnants, patterns of impact, and associated evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess protections and obligations for civilians under a party’s control
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether belligerents took steps to protect civilians and civilian objects under their control: constructing shelters, withdrawing civilians, avoiding locating military objectives in densely populated areas, removing civilians from vicinity of military objectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These obligations tie to the rule against use of human shields and to precautions; document measures (or lack thereof) taken by parties in controlled areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand elements of war crimes under the Rome Statute
rubrics_metrics.description: Know which serious violations of IHL are categorised as war crimes under Article 8 (e.g., grave breaches, attacks on civilians/objects, disproportionate attacks, pillaging, sexual violence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note ICC's higher culpability threshold: reckless or negligent attacks are generally not war crimes under the Statute, though indiscriminate or precaution-failing attacks may inform inferences about intent in certain circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess crimes against humanity: 'widespread' or 'systematic' attack criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: To evaluate crimes against humanity, determine whether acts formed part of an 'attack' pursuant to or in furtherance of a State or organisational policy and whether the attack was 'widespread' (scale/number of victims) or 'systematic' (organised, patterned conduct).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicators of systematic attack include political objective/plan, large-scale crimes against a civilian group, use of significant resources, and implication of high-level authorities. Collect pattern evidence: public statements, propaganda, administrative structures, repeated incidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess genocide and the special intent requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Know the acts that can constitute genocide (killing, causing serious harm, inflicting conditions to bring about destruction, measures to prevent births, forcible transfer of children) and that genocide requires specific intent to destroy a protected group 'as such'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate genocidal intent from other motivations; look for contextual indicators of intent (statements, policies, practices) and consult the Table of Factual Inquiries for indicative evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gather evidence about the mental element (intent and knowledge)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Article 30, material elements are only criminal if committed with intent and knowledge; Rome Statute offences cannot be committed recklessly (except in some domestic/customary contexts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate what the perpetrator knew, what they were actually trying to do, and why they acted (intercepted calls, orders, propaganda). Collect indirect indicators of intent: statements, patterns, targeting choices, methods used, and contextual evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Map command responsibility and control structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Map command and control lines and activities as superior/commander liability can arise from ordering, aiding/abetting, failing to prevent or punish crimes, or where superiors should have known (effective authority and control).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document hierarchies, communications, orders, and evidence of supervisory knowledge or negligence. This is important for attributing liability beyond direct perpetrators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collect public statements and contextual materials for pattern analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect and preserve political platforms, public statements, propaganda, administrative measures and other contextual evidence that may indicate a policy or organised plan behind attacks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patterns can be inferred from the totality of circumstances. Log and preserve statements and incidents to support allegations of widespread or systematic attacks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the Table of Factual Inquiries to drive case-specific questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Consult and apply the Table of Factual Inquiries as a practical checklist of relevant facts to seek, adjusting as appropriate to each case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Table organises common factual questions across crimes; you do not need to follow it sequentially—use judgement to expand/contract inquiries on a case-by-case basis and discuss pattern analysis with the legal team.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document incident location, time, and actors present
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish where the incident occurred, when it occurred, and who and what was present (including military activity, uniforms, badges, weapons, languages spoken, interviewees).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locate incidents in space/time (including multiple locations, e.g., MLRS barrages). Describe context such as background people, vehicle types, and on-scene interviews. Use available methods to establish time and geolocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document killings: victims, cause, perpetrators and evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: For killings, record who was killed (status as civilian/combatant, nationality, age, sex), where and when they were discovered, cause (including weapon type), who killed them, what they were doing when killed, and any evidence of motive or justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This information is core to many Rome Statute crimes; collect witness statements, justifications by attackers, and any corroborating material. Note relevance to intent and potential pattern analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document injuries and serious harm similarly to killings
rubrics_metrics.description: Record who was harmed, how they were harmed, who harmed them, where and when, and any evidence indicating why.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These inquiries mirror those for killings and are relevant to war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide investigations. Collect medical reports, survivor testimonies, imagery and other corroborating sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and document sexual and gender-based violence (SGBV) and red flags
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask who experienced SGBV, how many people, how they experienced it, who perpetrated it, and whether there is evidence of targeted reasons for assault.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the SGBV Annex for definitions and indicators. SGBV evidence may be sensitive—follow specialist guidance on handling, preserving and presenting such material.
